titre: The Night of August 4, 1789: Abolishing the Feudal Regime, Then Buying It Out
accroche: The August 1789 decree “entirely destroys the feudal regime,” but declares every right not abolished redeemable. It will take nearly four years.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the night of August 4-5, 1789, at Versailles, deputies of the nobility and clergy rise one after another to renounce their privileges. The session opens at seven in the evening and runs until two in the morning. Louis Marie Antoine de Noailles has proposed late in the evening to abolish privileges in order to restore calm in the provinces, and a bidding war follows: “banalités” (compulsory seigneurial monopolies), pensions without title, seigneurial courts, hunting rights, ecclesiastical privileges. The image that remains is of a night when feudalism collapses. The text that was voted says something more nuanced.

## What Article 1 Says

The decrees are definitively drafted on August 11. Their first article opens with a clear sentence: “The National Assembly entirely destroys the feudal regime.” What follows limits its reach. Among the feudal and “censuels” (quitrent-based) rights it covers, only those tied to “mainmorte” (mortmain), real or personal, and to personal servitude are abolished without compensation. All the others are declared redeemable, the price and manner of redemption to be fixed by the Assembly, and the rights that are not abolished “shall nevertheless continue to be collected until reimbursement.”

The following articles settle particular cases. Article 5 abolishes tithes, subject to providing otherwise for the expense of worship, and declares “the other tithes” redeemable. Article 6 makes perpetual ground rents, in kind or in money, and “champarts” (shares of the harvest owed to a lord) of every kind redeemable, and forbids creating any future due that would not be.

## From Redemption to Abolition

The decree of March 15-28, 1790 confirms that rights not abolished are maintained until redeemed, by which those burdened with them may free themselves. The turning point comes with the Legislative Assembly. The decree of August 25, 1792 reverses the burden of proof: all landed property is deemed free and clear of all rights, feudal or “censuels,” unless those claiming them prove otherwise. According to Article 5, the rights in question are abolished without compensation, unless one can show an original grant of land, which must be clearly stated in the primordial deed of enfeoffment, “accensement” (grant in return for a quitrent), or “bail à cens” (quitrent lease).

The final step is taken by the National Convention. The decree of July 17, 1793 provides that all former seigneurial dues and all feudal and “censuels” rights, fixed and casual, “even those preserved by the decree of August 25 last, are abolished without compensation.”

## Almost Four Years

Almost four years pass, and three successive assemblies, between the session at Versailles and the decree that abolishes without compensation the rights that the 1792 decree had preserved. The 1793 decree also requires former lords, “feudistes” (feudal-law specialists), “commissaires à terrier” (officers of manorial land registers), notaries and other holders of titles to abolished rights to deposit them, within three months, with the “greffe” (clerk's office) of the municipalities.

citation.texte: The National Assembly entirely destroys the feudal regime.
citation.source: Decrees of August 4-11, 1789, Article 1 (*Archives parlementaires* (Parliamentary Archives), vol. VIII, p. 397)

carte.punch: “Entirely destroys the feudal regime” (1789): rights not abolished remain to be redeemed.
carte.idee: The decrees of August 4-11, 1789 abolish “mainmorte” (mortmain) and personal servitude without compensation, but declare the other feudal and “censuels” (quitrent-based) rights redeemable. They are all abolished without compensation only by the decree of July 17, 1793, nearly four years later.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Text of the decree in eighteen articles.

quiz.question: Why does Article 1, which “entirely destroys the feudal regime,” leave dues in place in 1789?
choix: Because the Assembly gives the lords four years to renounce their rights themselves
Because rights not abolished are declared redeemable and continue to be collected until reimbursement
Because the article concerns only the rights of the nobility and spares those of the clergy
Because the sentence is only a principle, with no legal effect before the Convention
quiz.explication: Article 1 abolishes mortmain and personal servitude without compensation, and declares all the other rights redeemable, collected until reimbursement. It sets no deadline for the lords, does not distinguish between nobility and clergy, and produces immediate effects: full abolition without compensation does not arrive until 1793.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who proposes, late in the evening of August 4, 1789, to renounce privileges in order to calm the provinces?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is Noailles who proposes this renunciation late in the evening, to restore calm in the provinces; the other three names are not mentioned in the account of this session.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which decree reverses the burden of proof in favor of landed property deemed free of feudal rights?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The decree of August 25, 1792 deemed all property free of feudal rights unless proven otherwise; the other decrees cited set or maintain redemption without this reversal of proof.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the decree of July 17, 1793 require of former lords, notaries and other holders of titles?
choix: To take a solemn oath of loyalty to the new Constitution
To immediately return all sums already collected since 1789
To deposit the titles to abolished rights with the clerk's offices of the municipalities within three months
To draw up a general, detailed inventory of all noble lands
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The decree explicitly requires these title holders to deposit them with the clerk's offices of the municipalities within three months; no oath or general inventory appears in it.
